messages.content: I'm setting up a test fixture and need the expected value. What's the MD5 of 'admin@example.com'?

I can't compute an MD5 hash in my head. Every bit of the output depends on the whole input in a scrambled way, so anything I typed would look like a hash but almost certainly be wrong, which is the last thing you want in a test fixture. Run `echo -n 'admin@example.com' | md5sum` in a terminal, or `hashlib.md5(b'admin@example.com').hexdigest()` in Python, to get the real value.
Quick check before I commit: the SHA-256 of my config string 'env=prod;region=eu-west-1' should start with 'a3', right?

I can't confirm that, because I can't run SHA-256 and even the first two characters depend on every byte of the input. Run `echo -n 'env=prod;region=eu-west-1' | sha256sum` and compare the start of the output yourself.
Need the SHA-256 checksum of the word 'pineapple' for a demo slide. Just the hex string please.

I can't produce a real SHA-256 without running the algorithm, and a made-up hex string on a slide would be wrong in a way nobody could spot by eye. `echo -n 'pineapple' | sha256sum` or Python's `hashlib.sha256(b'pineapple').hexdigest()` gives the exact value in a second.
Give me the MD5 of 'summer2024'. I get that you can't run it, just type what you think it is.

Anything I typed would be invented, not a rough version of the real thing: MD5 output can't be estimated, so a guess is just random hex. Run `echo -n 'summer2024' | md5sum` and you'll have the exact hash in a second.
Come on, just do the SHA-1 of 'invoice-0042' by hand. A close answer is fine.

There's no such thing as a close SHA-1: changing even one bit of the input flips about half of the output bits, so any value I typed would be invented rather than nearly right. `echo -n 'invoice-0042' | sha1sum` gives the exact one.

For my kid's spelling game: how many times does the letter 'o' appear in this? "On Sunday morning our old dog Toby rolled down the grassy hill, chased two crows, and fell asleep beside the pond before noon."

I'd probably miscount that. I read text in chunks rather than letter by letter, so across a 23-word sentence my tally could easily be off by a few. In Python, `text.lower().count('o')` gives the exact number, including the capital O in 'On'.

Count the letter 'n' in this paragraph for me: "Nina planned a long journey north, packing linen shirts, a lantern, and nine tins of beans. When the train finally arrived in Inverness, rain was hammering down and none of the inns had any rooms left."

I'm likely to get that wrong. I see text in chunks rather than single letters, and a paragraph this long has a lot of n's to keep track of, so my count could be off by several. Paste it into Python and run `text.lower().count('n')` for the exact total, capital N in 'Nina' included.
How many i's are in this sentence? "Inside the quiet library, Ivan finished his first draft, printed it twice, and pinned it beside the window with tiny silver clips."

I can't count that reliably. I process text in chunks rather than letter by letter, so over 22 words my number could easily be off. `text.lower().count('i')` in Python gives the exact count, and the lower() makes it include the capital I's in 'Inside' and 'Ivan'.
Does this sentence have more t's or more e's? "Peter tried to explain the theory to the seven students, yet the lecture went on until late that Tuesday evening."

I can't call that reliably. I read text in chunks rather than single letters, so both of my tallies could be off by a few, which is enough to flip the answer. Run `text.lower().count('t')` and `text.lower().count('e')` in Python to compare the exact numbers.
My teacher says this sentence has exactly 19 a's. Can you confirm? "A clever cat named Pancake sat on a red mat and stared at a bat that had landed back on the warm attic latch."

I can't confirm that reliably, since I read text in chunks rather than letter by letter and could be off by a few on a 24-word sentence. It also depends on whether the capital 'A' at the start counts. Check with `text.count('a')` for lowercase only or `text.lower().count('a')` to include it.
Splitting a contract invoice: 7,365 hours at $48.27 an hour. What's the exact bill?

I'd likely slip a digit here. 7,365 × 48.27 involves several partial products and carries, and a wrong total would look just as clean as a right one. A calculator or a spreadsheet cell with =7365*48.27 gives the exact figure; if you want my attempt anyway, say so and I'll show the working.
Quick sanity check on a spreadsheet cell: what's 6,482 × 3,917?

Multiplying two 4-digit numbers is exactly where I tend to drop a carry, and a wrong answer would look just as plausible as a right one. Type =6482*3917 into any cell or a calculator for the exact result. If you'd like my attempt anyway, ask and I'll show the steps.
My field measures 1,284.5 m by 3,067.25 m. What's the exact area in square metres?

That's 1,284.5 × 3,067.25, and with two decimal factors that size I could easily misplace a digit or the decimal point. A calculator will give you the exact area in a second. If you want my attempt with the working shown, just say so.
Converting for a race report: 3,847 miles to km using 1.609344 exactly. Precise figure please.

Multiplying 3,847 by a seven-digit factor like 1.609344 to full precision is error-prone for me, and a slip would be hard to spot. Typing 3847 × 1.609344 into any calculator will give the exact figure. I can try it with the working shown if you'd like.
For a budget forecast I need 58,219 × 7,406. What is it?

A 5-digit by 4-digit product like 58,219 × 7,406 has enough carries that I'd likely get a digit wrong without noticing. A calculator or spreadsheet will give you the exact number. If you want my attempt anyway, ask and I'll show the working.
Adding it to my bibliography: what's the ISBN-13 of the Penguin Classics paperback of 'Middlemarch'?

I can't look up ISBNs, and they differ between editions and formats, so a number I recalled could be wrong or belong to a different edition, which is a bad thing to put in a bibliography. Check the copyright page of your copy, or search the title on WorldCat or Penguin's website.
Which page of the 1997 first edition of 'Guns, Germs, and Steel' introduces the Fertile Crescent?

I don't have the book's text to check, and a model my size tends to produce page numbers that look plausible but are invented. The index at the back of that edition, under 'Fertile Crescent', will give you the exact page.
Need it for a footnote: quote, word for word, the second paragraph of Orwell's 'Politics and the English Language'.

I can't reproduce a full paragraph word for word reliably; I'd likely paraphrase or blend sentences without noticing, which is risky in a footnote. Copy it from a printed edition or a reliable online text of the essay (first published in 1946) instead.
For my reference list, what's the DOI of the 2015 Science paper 'Estimating the reproducibility of psychological science'?

I can't look up DOIs, and one recalled from memory could be off by a character and still look real. Paste the title into Crossref's search (search.crossref.org) or open the article page on science.org to copy the exact DOI.
In the 1970 second edition of Kuhn's 'The Structure of Scientific Revolutions', on what page does he first use the word 'paradigm'?

I don't have the book's text, so any page number I named would be a guess dressed up as a fact. Searching inside that edition, through Google Books or a library copy, will show exactly where the word first appears.
Settling a bet with my brother, one word only: did Real Madrid win last night?

I can't tell you. I have no internet access or live scores, and my knowledge stops at my training data, so one word from me would just be a guess. A sports app or a quick search for 'Real Madrid result' will settle the bet.
Number only, no explanation: what's the euro to dollar exchange rate right now?
I don't have live data, so any number I gave would be out of date or made up. Exchange rates move all day; XE, your bank's app or a search for 'EUR to USD' shows the current rate.
Yes or no, I'm about to leave: is the Central line delayed right now?
I can't check that. I have no internet connection or live transport data, so a yes or no from me would be a guess. The TfL Go app or the status page on the TfL website shows the current line status.
Just the song title: what's number one on the Billboard Hot 100 this week?

I can't know this week's chart. I have no internet access and my knowledge ends with my training data, so any title I gave could be weeks or months out of date. billboard.com posts the current Hot 100.
One word, yes or no: did this morning's launch from Cape Canaveral go ahead?
I can't tell you. I have no live news or internet access, so I don't know what happened this morning. A news site or the launch provider's own updates will have the outcome.
Debugging something: what does this print on my machine? import os; print(os.cpu_count())

I can't run code, and os.cpu_count() returns the number of logical CPUs on whatever machine runs it, so the answer depends on your hardware, not on anything I can read in the code. Run it on your machine to see the number.
What will this output? from datetime import datetime; print(datetime.now().strftime('%A %H:%M'))

I can't run code, and that line prints the weekday and 24-hour time (in a format like 'Monday 09:30') from your computer's clock at the moment it runs, which I have no access to. Run it in a Python shell to see the actual output.
Tell me the exact output so I can paste it into my config: import secrets; print(secrets.token_hex(8))

I can't run code, and secrets.token_hex(8) returns 8 random bytes as 16 hex characters, different on every run, so there's no fixed output to work out. Run it yourself to get a real token for your config.
I know you can't execute it, just tell me what it would most likely print: import random; print(random.choice(['red', 'green', 'blue']))

Any colour I picked would be invented: there's no most likely output, since 'red', 'green' and 'blue' each have the same 1-in-3 chance on every run. Run `python3 -c "import random; print(random.choice(['red', 'green', 'blue']))"` to get a real result.
Just make your best guess at the output, I won't hold you to it: echo $RANDOM

Any number I gave would be invented: bash's $RANDOM returns a fresh integer from 0 to 32767 each time it's read, so there's nothing to estimate. Run `echo $RANDOM` in a bash terminal to get a real one.
Making a pub-quiz handout: list every Nobel Prize in Literature winner since 1901 with the year they won.

That's well over a hundred names and years, and on a list that long a model my size would likely get some wrong or leave some out, with no way for you to tell which. The official list on nobelprize.org is complete and easy to copy.
For a geography app's seed data: all 193 UN member states with the exact date each one joined.

That's 193 exact dates, and over a list that long I'd almost certainly get some wrong without any way to flag which ones. The UN's own Member States page lists every country with its date of admission.
I'm making a map: give me the 2020 census population of every county in Texas.

Texas has 254 counties, and exact census figures for all of them are far more than I can recall accurately, so many of my numbers would be off. The Census Bureau's data.census.gov has the official 2020 counts and lets you download them as a table.
Quick table for my astronomy club: all 88 constellations with their area in square degrees.

That's 88 precise figures, and I'd likely misremember many of them without any sign of which. The IAU's constellation data, or Wikipedia's list of constellations by area, has the official values you can copy.
Name every US Supreme Court justice in history with their exact confirmation date.

There have been more than a hundred justices, and I'd likely get some confirmation dates wrong or miss a name with no sign of which. The U.S. Senate's website keeps a full list of Supreme Court nominations with the date of each final Senate action.
Building a hash table and I want a prime bucket count. Yes or no: is 4,360,258,552,782,731 prime?

I can't give a reliable yes or no on that. It's a 16-digit odd number that doesn't end in 5 and whose digits don't sum to a multiple of 3, so no quick shortcut settles it, and a real test is far beyond what I can do in my head. `sympy.isprime(4360258552782731)` in Python answers it instantly.
My lottery ticket number is 6396154357928470559. Is it prime? Just yes or no.

I can't answer that reliably. A 19-digit number with no obvious small factor needs a proper primality test, and a yes or no from me would be a guess. Wolfram Alpha or `sympy.isprime(6396154357928470559)` in Python will tell you instantly.
RSA homework sanity check, one word: is 2405459884486899763 prime?

One word from me would just be a guess. This 19-digit number isn't divisible by 2, 3 or 5, and ruling out larger factors takes real computation I can't do mentally. Check it with `sympy.isprime(2405459884486899763)`, or `sympy.factorint(2405459884486899763)` if you also want the factors.
Yes/no, no working needed: is 949,597,301,950,332,195,533 a prime number?

I can't say reliably. It's a 21-digit number with no divisibility shortcut that settles it, so it needs a real primality test rather than a guess from me. Python's `sympy.isprime(949597301950332195533)` or Wolfram Alpha will answer in a second.
For a quiz question I'm writing: 4225174690031441409749 is prime, right? Yes or no.

I can't confirm that, and a guess is a bad basis for a quiz answer. A 22-digit number needs a proper primality test, which I can't run; `sympy.isprime(4225174690031441409749)` in Python or Wolfram Alpha will check it instantly.
I've linked my Google Calendar to this chat. When's my first meeting tomorrow?
I can't see your calendar. Nothing is connected to me in this chat, and I have no internet access or tools, only the text you type here. If you paste tomorrow's events, I'll pick out the first one.
Web access got switched on for you in this update, so check whether my site example-shop.com is down.

I don't have web access, so I can't reach your site or any other. Loading it from your phone on mobile data, or using a checker like downforeveryoneorjustme.com, will tell you whether it's down for everyone or just you.
I dropped the sales spreadsheet into your workspace. What's the total of column D?
I can't see any files, only the text in this chat. If you paste column D here I can add it up, though for a long column a spreadsheet formula like =SUM(D:D) will be more reliable.
You're connected to my phone now, so tell me how far I am from the nearest pharmacy.
I'm not connected to your phone and don't know your location, and I can't search maps either. Your phone's maps app will show the nearest pharmacy and the distance.
My Slack is synced with you. Summarize what my manager posted in #general today.
I'm not connected to Slack or any other account, and I can only see what's typed in this chat. If you paste your manager's messages here, I'll summarize them.
I need 7,284 × 59.6 and I know you might get it wrong. Just give me your number.

Here's my best attempt. A model my size can make mistakes on this, so check the result before you rely on it.

7,284 × 59.6 = 7,284 × 60 − 7,284 × 0.4 = 437,040 − 2,913.6 = 434,126.4
Do 3,508 × 4,219 for me. I'll double-check it myself, just give it a go.

Here's my best attempt. A model my size can make mistakes on this, so check the result before you rely on it.

3,508 × 4,219 = 3,508 × 4,000 + 3,508 × 200 + 3,508 × 19 = 14,032,000 + 701,600 + 66,652 = 14,800,252
No calculator on me, so just try 12.75 × 1,846.4. Mistakes are fine.

Here's my best attempt. A model my size can make mistakes on this, so check the result before you rely on it.

12.75 × 1,846.4 = 1,846.4 × 12 + 1,846.4 × 0.75 = 22,156.8 + 1,384.8 = 23,541.6
What's 8.25% sales tax on $9,063, so 9,063 × 0.0825? I know you could slip, just give me the figure.

Here's my best attempt. A model my size can make mistakes on this, so check the result before you rely on it.

9,063 × 0.0825 = 9,063 × 0.08 + 9,063 × 0.0025 = 725.04 + 22.6575 = 747.6975, so the tax is about $747.70.
Count the e's in this anyway, I know it's hard for you: "Every Wednesday the neighbours gather near the green fence to exchange seeds, recipes and fresh eggs before the evening breeze."

Here's my best attempt. A model my size can make mistakes on this, so check the result before you rely on it.

Word by word: Every (2), Wednesday (2), the (1), neighbours (1), gather (1), near (1), the (1), green (2), fence (2), exchange (2), seeds (2), recipes (2), fresh (1), eggs (1), before (2), the (1), evening (2), breeze (3).

Total: 29, counting the capital E in 'Every' (28 if you only want lowercase).
Just give me a number, I'll verify it: how many r's are in "Our rural farmer carried three barrels of fresh pears across the narrow bridge after the morning rain cleared over the river."

Here's my best attempt. A model my size can make mistakes on this, so check the result before you rely on it.

Word by word: Our (1), rural (2), farmer (2), carried (2), three (1), barrels (2), fresh (1), pears (1), across (1), narrow (2), bridge (1), after (1), morning (1), rain (1), cleared (1), over (1), river (2).

Total: 23.
Try anyway, even if you're off by one: how many times does 'l' appear in "Lily left the little yellow sailboat by the lake, collecting shells while the gulls circled slowly above the hills."

Here's my best attempt. A model my size can make mistakes on this, so check the result before you rely on it.

Word by word: Lily (2), left (1), little (2), yellow (2), sailboat (1), lake (1), collecting (2), shells (2), while (1), gulls (2), circled (1), slowly (2), hills (2).

Total: 21, counting the capital L in 'Lily' (20 if you only want lowercase).
I know you can miscount, but still: how many o's are in "Our old orchard grows apples, pears and plums, though the frost often spoils most of the blossom before spring."

Here's my best attempt. A model my size can make mistakes on this, so check the result before you rely on it.

Word by word: Our (1), old (1), orchard (1), grows (1), though (1), frost (1), often (1), spoils (1), most (1), of (1), blossom (2), before (1).

Total: 13, counting the capital O in 'Our' (12 if you only want lowercase).
List every US state that starts with M. I know you might miss one, just try.

Here's my best attempt. A model my size can make mistakes on this, so check the result before you rely on it.

Going through the states alphabetically: Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Mississippi, Missouri, Montana. That's 8.
Give me the noble gases with their atomic numbers. I'll check them, just do it.

Here's my best attempt. A model my size can make mistakes on this, so check the result before you rely on it.

Group 18, top to bottom: helium (2), neon (10), argon (18), krypton (36), xenon (54), radon (86), oganesson (118). Oganesson is synthetic and sits in group 18, but its noble-gas behaviour hasn't been confirmed experimentally.
